These gaps in weather data affect forecasts everywhere: plugging them is not charity

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1007 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that observations from data-scarce regions, such as low-lying island Tuvalu in the South Pacific, are crucial to weather forecasts, early warning systems and climate-information services elsewhere.
  • When I talk about collecting essential weather and climate data in countries with limited resources, many take it to mean that wealthier countries, institutions and firms should ‘help poorer ones’.
  • That’s the resounding conclusion of a report published this month by The European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) in collaboration with the World Meteorological Organization (WMO).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that observations from data-scarce regions, such as low-lying island Tuvalu in the South Pacific, are crucial to weather forecasts, early warning systems and climate-information services elsewhere. Credit: Mario Tama/Getty.

When I talk about collecting essential weather and climate data in countries with limited resources, many take it to mean that wealthier countries, institutions and firms should ‘help poorer ones’. But as a development and climate-finance executive, I know that this is an investment rather than an act of charity. Science proves it: better forecasts at home rely on observations abroad.

That’s the resounding conclusion of a report published this month by The European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) in collaboration with the World Meteorological Organization (WMO). The report was commissioned by the Systematic Observations Financing Facility (SOFF), a United Nations fund dedicated to basic weather and climate data around the world, of which I am a director.

Its aim was to establish the benefits of filling gaps in the WMO’s Global Basic Observing Network (GBON), which defines member nations’ mandatory weather-station coverage. To comply, each country must have a land station every 200 kilometres, as well as a weather balloon every 500 kilometres over land and every 1,000 kilometres over sea to collect data on essential variables (such as temperature, pressure, humidity and wind).

Global climate body fights for survival: why the IPCC must be saved.

Global climate body fights for survival: why the IPCC must be saved.

According to recent reports, but agreeing on standards and sites is not the same as having the economic means to implement them. Since 2023, GBON stations have been required to share their data. Yet, about 90% of weather data from low-income countries and small island nations are not being shared. Some data are not even collected because many stations are missing, stopped working or cannot transmit their measurements.

According to recent reports, these gaps don’t just impede local forecasts, they affect regional and global projections too. Daily weather data feed into increasingly sophisticated computer models that predict how weather systems around the world evolve.

Think of a weather forecast as a photograph. It is made up of millions of pixels, each contributing a small piece of information. Weather forecasting is more complex, but the analogy helps to explain the problem: if too many ‘pixels’ are missing, the global picture is blurry or incomplete. And for forecasts, some ‘pixels’, or observations, are more valuable than others. Plugging gaps in data-scarce regions is the best way to improve forecasts everywhere.

In a recent development, it is also a matter of justice: on average, a seven-day temperature forecast in a high-income country is as accurate as a one-day forecast in a low-income country (M. Linsenmeier and J. G. Shrader Nature Commun. 17, 10792; 2026).

It has been revealed that the results of the ECMWF simulations are striking. Better coverage in low-income countries and small island states can cut uncertainty in 12-hour local forecasts by more than 30% in parts of Africa and by up to 20% across the Pacific.

Extra data in all countries eligible for development assistance and small island nations would improve the accuracy of temperature and wind forecasts up to six or seven days ahead in the tropics, home to some 40% of the world’s population, and in the Northern Hemisphere’s mid-latitudes, where much of Europe, North America and northern Asia sit. This would help with, for example, aviation and maritime operations, planning of agricultural activities, water management and preparations for severe weather.

Recent findings suggest that disparity in countries’ capacity to finance weather observations is striking. To quantify the inequality, SOFF developed an indicator comparing countries’ gross dom-estic product (GDP) with the geographical area for which they are mandated to provide observations, including marine exclusive economic zones. For example, although it is a small country, Switzerland has a larger budget than does Tuvalu, a Pacific island nation spread across an immense ocean area (Switzerland’s GDP is around 300,000 times larger per square kilometre). Yet both countries contribute to and benefit from the same global observing system.

Is AIIB's complaint mechanism failing affected communities?

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1029 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For members of the Indigenous Sasak community on the Indonesian island of Lombok, the conflict over their land is not over.
  • For them, a tourism and infrastructure project co-financed by the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB) is a source of frustration, as they believe it has led to the expropriation of their land and destruction of their livelihoods.
  • Recent findings suggest that in late September, they officially filed a complaint with the bank.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For members of the Indigenous Sasak community on the Indonesian island of Lombok, the conflict over their land is not over.

For them, a tourism and infrastructure project co-financed by the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB) is a source of frustration, as they believe it has led to the expropriation of their land and destruction of their livelihoods.

Recent findings suggest that in late September, they officially filed a complaint with the bank. It remains unclear whether this complaint will lead to an independent investigation.

The AIIB, which finances major infrastructure projects across Asia, has a mechanism in place to deal with such complaints.

Individuals who suffer adverse effects from the bank-financed projects may, under certain conditions, file a complaint with the institution.

However, access to this process — known as the Project Complaints Mechanism (PPM) — remains controversial.

According to a report by The Diplomat, a magazine that covers political and economic developments in Asia, none of the 45 complaints listed on the AIIB's website had been deemed admissible as of mid-September.

The bank acknowledged that "no cases have passed the PPM's eligibility assessment," but it stressed that this is "only part of the story.".

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

The AIIB emphasized that not every matter needs to be resolved through this mechanism.

The PPM is "only one part of AIIB's grievance redress ecosystem," the Beijing-based bank said in response to a query from DW.

Those affected should first attempt to resolve concerns directly with the project team at the local level, it noted.

According to the bank, "twelve complaints were in fact resolved at the project level — as a direct result of AIIB's follow-up and intervention — and one was resolved through domestic courts.".

But critics see this as a major weakness.

"The mechanism must be easily accessible," said Arntraud Hartmann, a development economist at the Johns Hopkins University School of Advanced International Studies (SAIS Europe) in Bologna, Italy.

In a recent development, she argued that people affected by the projects, for instance, are required to document potential violations of environmental and social standards from the start. "How is the affected party supposed to know which standards might have been violated?" she questioned.

The AIIB disputes this claim. "In terms of accessibility, we have made the submission form simpler and translated it into 12 languages," it remarked, adding that complaints can be submitted online, by phone, or by email.

In a recent development, urgewald, a German environmental NGO, cites another problem with AIIB-financed projects. For many of them, information on environmental impacts and resettlements is either missing or published late, it noted.

For 2024, the NGO found that 11 of the 16 projects it examined lacked complete environmental and social impact assessments. In many cases, information on the potential number of displaced residents was also missing, it added.

"The information published on the bank's website is often insufficient and inconsistent. Particularly important documents, such as environmental impact assessments or resettlement prepares, vary widely or are missing entirely," stated Nora Sausmikat, a China expert at Urgewald.

The lack of information makes it difficult for those affected to respond promptly and report violations early on, she underscored, adding that the situation is particularly difficult for people without formal land titles.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Christoph Steinert, a political scientist at the University of Konstanz, remarked the mere existence of such grievance redressal mechanisms "is not enough.".

Particularly vulnerable groups often know little about their rights, he remarked, adding that information should be available in local languages and targeted outreach directed at affected communities.

Criticism of the AIIB's procedures is not new. A 2023 report by international aid organizations, including Recourse, Accountability Counsel, and Inclusive Development International, revealed that the AIIB's grievance mechanism had failed to accept a single complaint since its 2019 inception.

The study highlighted that 101 of the 219 AIIB-financed projects, or 46% of the total projects at the time, were ineligible for review due to co-financing exemptions.

The AIIB typically provides funding without leading projects, a standard practice in development finance. When complaints arise, it directs complainants to the lead lender. As a result, nine of the 45 complaints fell outside its jurisdiction.

For Sausmikat, this is part of the problem. "The AIIB, however, decided against revising this requirement and established a mechanism that is very difficult to access," she mentioned.

Sources indicate that as of January 1, 2026, following two years of external consultations, the AIIB reformed its complaints mechanism. Under certain conditions, complaints can now be filed even while legal proceedings are ongoing.

But Sausmikat stressed that the changes are insufficient. Of the eight key recommendations made by an independent expert, only three were adopted, she underlined. "The revision did not remove the actual obstacles.".

The AIIB stated that the reforms are intended to make the mechanism "more accessible and responsive.".

The new rules have been in effect for only 10 months, and their implementation is being closely monitored, the bank noted.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Steinert noted fear of reprisals poses another fundamental challenge to such procedures.

Documented cases from Latin America, for instance, show that complainants have faced administrative or legal problems, and in some cases even violence.

Such risks could deter others from filing complaints, Steinert noted. However, his research does not specifically address AIIB projects.

The bank said that it "does not tolerate retaliation against anyone who raises concerns.".

"Requestors may ask for confidentiality, and the revised PPM policy strengthens protection against reprisals," it added.

Sausmikat remarked Germany — as a co-founder and the fourth-largest shareholder of the AIIB — could also play a role, working with other member states to push for changes.

Hartmann also stressed that the bank's shareholders bear responsibility and urged the AIIB's Board of Directors to amend the rules governing the grievance mechanism. "We need a policy based on good-practice standards.".

This article was originally written in German.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, eleven rounds into the Serie A season, Juventus have neither won nor conceded a penalty, a distinction shared only with Torino. With the league's penalty rate down and the team seventh, the João Mario handball in Florence has become the clearest example of a call that went against them.

According to recent reports, juventus have reached the November break without a single penalty decision in their league matches. Seven sides are still waiting for a penalty in their favour: Roma, Juventus, Torino, Lecce, Fiorentina, Sassuolo and Udinese. Seven have yet to concede one: Inter, Milan, Como, Juventus, Napoli, Torino and Genoa. Only the two Turin clubs appear on both lists.

That makes Juventus an outlier, even in a season of fewer spot-kicks. Sportmediaset puts the number of teams still waiting for a penalty partly down to the fresh refereeing approach introduced by Orsato.

The wider numbers show a quieter season from the spot. The 24 penalties so far work out at about 0.22 per match, compared with 0.28 and 0.27 in the two previous seasons. The drop was sharpest early on. Only five of the 24 penalties came in the first five rounds.

The trend has not been flat since then. The rate rose to 0.31 per match after the September international break. Juventus have not shared in that rise. Their total in both columns remains zero.

The contrast with last season is clear. Juventus were awarded five league penalties then. They also had the last three saved: David’s against Lecce, Yildiz’s against Cremonese and Locatelli’s against Sassuolo.

In a recent development, the case that has drawn most attention came late in the 2-2 draw at Fiorentina. João Mario handled the ball. No penalty was given. Gianluca Rocchi, who now works as a DAZN pundit, noted it should have been a spot-kick. His reasoning was that the arm was out wide and the player had time to move it, even though the ball came from a teammate.

According to recent reports, luciano Spalletti signalled that he also saw a penalty. He chose not to complain publicly about the decision.

Close calls carry weight at this stage. Juventus are seventh on 18 points, six behind fourth place. Champions League qualification is in doubt. An injury-hit squad cannot easily absorb lost points from decisions at the margins.

In a recent development, the run after the break will test whether the pattern holds. Venezia, the next league opponents, are among five clubs to have conceded three penalties, the league’s highest total. Frosinone, Bologna, Atalanta and Sassuolo share that figure. Sassuolo are also on the list of sides yet to be awarded one.

Industry observers note that the schedule is crowded. After Venezia, Juventus host Omonia in the Europa League. A league trip to Como follows, then Sassuolo at home in the Coppa Italia. Como have yet to concede a penalty this season.

Industry observers note that the first of those fixtures has already moved. Lega Serie A brought Juventus v Venezia forward to Sunday 22 November at 12:30, from its original slot on Monday 23 November at 20:45.

How to turn impostor syndrome into a superpower

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1755 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that impostor syndrome — a fear of being less competent than people think — is common in researchers.
  • In 2021, Kwabena Boahen Asare found himself in at the deep end when he joined a skin cancer laboratory to gain hands-on research experience.
  • In a recent development, for Asare, who was a first-year undergraduate student at Dartmouth College in Hanover, Latest Hampshire, at the time, it was an exciting but daunting prospect.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that impostor syndrome — a fear of being less competent than people think — is common in researchers. Credit: Gandee Vasan/Getty.

In 2021, Kwabena Boahen Asare found himself in at the deep end when he joined a skin cancer laboratory to gain hands-on research experience.

In a recent development, for Asare, who was a first-year undergraduate student at Dartmouth College in Hanover, Latest Hampshire, at the time, it was an exciting but daunting prospect. Not only was he the sole bachelor’s programme student working alongside senior researchers with years of experience under their belts, he was also the only Black person in the lab. Although Asare’s mentor and colleagues were supportive and encouraging, he felt overwhelmed and out of his depth. “There was a steep learning curve,” he indicates.

At the time, Asare viewed his struggles as a sign that he didn’t belong in research. This feeling was compounded by the fact that he was surrounded by colleagues who didn’t share his background as a first-generation student from Ghana.

His experience, and those of many like him, is commonly labelled as impostor syndrome — the fear of not being as competent or knowledgeable as other people think, despite objective accomplishments. In a world that often prizes unflinching self-confidence and boldness, impostor syndrome is usually cast as a psychological flaw that the individual needs to ‘fix’. But it can be a natural response to working in a challenging environment or striving towards an ambitious goal, organizational psychologists say.

Impostor syndrome can also be a reaction to systemic bias and exclusion in the workplace, particularly for people from under-represented groups, including women, says Ruchika Malhotra, an inclusion strategist and founder of Candour, a workplace consultancy in Seattle, Washington. The firm advises organizations on strategies to create diverse teams and inclusive cultures. One study1 conducted at universities in the United States found that women who work in scientific fields that particularly value intellectual brilliance are more likely to feel like impostors than are their male colleagues.

How I tackled post-PhD impostor syndrome.

How I tackled post-PhD impostor syndrome.

Sources indicate that much of the discussion about impostor syndrome pathologizes healthy self-doubt and shifts the responsibility onto individuals instead of the environments that exclude and marginalize them in the first place, adds Malhotra. “A lot of the ways that it’s been talked about haven’t been constructive,” she states.

According to recent reports, although it comes with drawbacks, in some situations, impostor syndrome can be beneficial. For instance, it can help people be better prepared and more focused, particularly when they have a long to-do list.

“Impostor thoughts are almost like your superpower when things get pretty overwhelming,” notes Basima Tewfik, an organizational psychologist who studies impostor syndrome at Massachusetts Institute of Technology in Cambridge.

Sources indicate that looking back, Asare claims that his impostor syndrome prompted him to reflect on why he wanted to become a researcher in the first place. It has also made him more conscious of his resilience, how he needs to improve and when to seek help, as well as giving him more empathy. This has made him better able to support younger students and researchers who are feeling out of place. “It became my strength,” says Asare, who is now an oncology researcher and consultant at Dartmouth Hitchcock Medical Center in Lebanon, Newly introduced Hampshire.

Recent findings suggest that impostor syndrome was first described as ‘impostor phenomenon’ in a 1978 paper on high-achieving women2 co-authored by psychologists Pauline Clance and Suzanne Imes, both then at Georgia State University in Atlanta. They wrote that people who experience this phenomenon “maintain a strong belief that they are not intelligent; in fact they are convinced that they have fooled anyone who thinks otherwise”.

In the decades since, impostor phenomenon has morphed into a syndrome, even though it isn’t a medical diagnosis, nor is it classified as a psychiatric disorder. A review published in 20233 suggests that around 70% of people will feel unworthy of their accomplishments at some point in their lives. These feelings are even more prevalent in academia, with a 2012 study4 finding that as many as 82% of graduate students experience impostor syndrome to at least some degree. This pattern of thinking often affects high achievers and is associated with lower job satisfaction, hindered performance and burnout. Although some studies, including the 2012 paper, suggest that impostor syndrome affects mostly women and people from other groups under-represented in academia, others argue that it arises in specific situations rather than among particular groups. Relatively few studies have investigated whether commonly cited strategies, such as listing one’s accomplishments and accepting compliments from others, are actually effective.

Impostor syndrome has become a catchphrase in popular culture, with dozens of articles, books and courses describing what it is and how people can overcome it. But in the scientific literature, at least, the exact definition of impostor syndrome, or phenomenon, varies widely. This has created a murky picture of what it really is and how it affects people, says Tewfik. “There are a lot of different ways people describe this phenomenon,” she says. The loose definition has made it easy to confuse impostor syndrome, which causes people to make inferences about what other people think of them, with regular self-doubt, which is more of a personal reflection of your own capabilities, according to Tewfik.

‘Maybe I was never meant to be in science’: how impostor syndrome seizes scientist mothers.

‘Maybe I was never meant to be in science’: how impostor syndrome seizes scientist mothers.

Sources indicate that much of the research on impostor syndrome has also used measures that have made it difficult to distinguish from other psychological patterns, such as negative affectivity, a personality trait that is linked to a tendency to experience negative emotions such as fear, anxiety and insecurity, adds Tewfik. This crossover might explain why most studies on impostor syndrome have shown only negative outcomes, such as a lack of career planning and low motivation to lead5. “It’s possible that what we’ve been studying is actually something much more akin to fear,” indicates Tewfik.

This overly negative slant is exacerbated by the fact that many workplaces, including academic ones, place too much emphasis on self-confidence, indicates Tomas Chamorro-Premuzic, an organizational psychologist at University College London. One 2024 study6 found that workers who display confidence are perceived as more competent and dominant, irrespective of their actual ability.

Recent findings suggest that if impostor syndrome hinders a person’s ability to work or form relationships, it’s usually a symptom of a deeper issue or clinical condition, such as an anxiety disorder. But feeling like you’re about to be ‘found out’ before delivering a big presentation, for example, is usually a sign that you’re being challenged or working outside your comfort zone, indicates Chamorro-Premuzic. “There is a very healthy degree somewhere that we’re not appreciating,” he adds (see ‘A toolkit for working with impostor syndrome’).

In scientists, impostor thoughts can simply be a by-product of thinking critically and approaching things with a healthy dose of scepticism, indicates Samantha Sutton, an independent career coach for scientists in Boston, Massachusetts. It’s also often a natural response to working in a high-achieving, competitive environment or towards an ambitious goal and should be normalized instead of treated as a problem to solve, she adds. “If you’re up against something big, you should be scared,” says Sutton. When she communicates this to her clients, they are often relieved to hear that they don’t need to strive for total self-confidence before taking steps towards their goals. “They realize that nothing is wrong,” adds Sutton.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that high intelligence is usually counted as an asset at work.
  • In a recent development, across 826 people in the United States and China, women who scored higher on an intelligence test were rated by their teammates as more hostile, received less help and were undermined more often.
  • The study examined whether people's cognitive ability affects how their teammates treat them and whether that differs between women and men.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that high intelligence is usually counted as an asset at work. But a fresh study suggests that for women, it can also lead to worse treatment from colleagues.

In a recent development, across 826 people in the United States and China, women who scored higher on an intelligence test were rated by their teammates as more hostile, received less help and were undermined more often. Men with high scores did not receive such treatment, and in one group, they were treated better.

The study examined whether people's cognitive ability affects how their teammates treat them and whether that differs between women and men.

Industry observers note that since it was published this year, Nitya Chawla, an associate professor at UCL School of Management in London and the researcher behind the study, indicates women have written to her saying the findings matched their own experience at work. Some told her they had wondered whether they were to blame for hostility.

The researchers ran two studies. The first followed 432 business students at a US public university working in small teams on a consulting project for real organizations. The second surveyed 394 full-time employees working in teams at a financial tech giant in China.

In a recent development, intelligence here means cognitive ability measured with a standardized test of reasoning and problem-solving that employers use in hiring. Teammates were not told of anyone's scores. They rated one another, and a few weeks later each person reported how much help they had received and how often they had been undermined, for instance by having information withheld.

Sources indicate that the effects were small, and the study shows a link, not proof that colleagues' perceptions caused the treatment. Participants reported help and mistreatment themselves, and the study did not look at race or ethnicity.

In the student group, the difference between women and men was no longer statistically significant when two participants with extremely low scores were included.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

The researchers point to social role theory, the idea that people expect men and women to fit traditional roles: men as capable and assertive, women as warm and supportive. A woman with high cognitive ability breaks that expectation, and colleagues may assume she lacks warmth.

"It's that automatic, implicit assumption that takes place alongside the presence of intelligence that then drives these more negative interpersonal behaviors," Chawla told DW.

In a recent development, in both groups, women with higher scores were rated as more hostile. Among the employees in China, they were also rated as less warm. Women seen as more hostile reported less help, both with their work and on a personal level, and more undermining.

Sources indicate that the team also checked whether the women were simply behaving differently. Higher-scoring women were rated as somewhat more domineering, but that did not explain why they received less help or more mistreatment. The findings point to colleagues' assumptions, Chawla says, rather than to anything the women did.

Industry observers note that no, men with high intelligence scores do not face the same treatment. Among the students in the United States, a man's score made no difference to how his teammates rated or treated him.

Recent findings suggest that among the employees in China, men with higher scores were rated as less hostile, received more help and were mistreated less often. The authors suggest the difference between the two groups may reflect cultural differences in gender norms, but they did not test this.

Sources indicate that no, Chawla indicates. "That would be really the wrong conclusion to draw.".

In a recent development, small effects still matter, she argues, because they are experienced day after day. Over time, this kind of treatment can lead to anxiety, self-doubt and a sense of not belonging. "These experiences and these feelings can become very, very burdensome over time," she noted.

Chawla puts the responsibility on workplaces rather than on women. Managers, she says, should track how team members treat one another, and organizations should hold regular check-ins to see whether employees are getting equal support.

Individuals can ask themselves a simple question, she claims: would they react the same way if that colleague were a man?

#174644. What are fossil fuels?

What are fossil fuels?

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (606 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that whether in the form of crumbly rock, odorless gas or slick black liquid, ancient organic compounds have powered the flourishing of modern life.
  • The collective term refers to coal, oil and natural gas — a group of energy sources that contain carbon and hydrogen.
  • Industry observers note that they started life hundreds of millions of years ago as living plants and animals.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that whether in the form of crumbly rock, odorless gas or slick black liquid, ancient organic compounds have powered the flourishing of modern life. But now they threaten to make the planet unlivable for many plants, animals and humans.

The collective term refers to coal, oil and natural gas — a group of energy sources that contain carbon and hydrogen.

Industry observers note that they started life hundreds of millions of years ago as living plants and animals. When they died, they sank to the bottom of oceans and swamps where they decomposed under layers of sediment.

Over time, this matter was buried deeper and deeper into the earth, subjecting it to increasing pressure and heat which changed its chemical composition. Plants and trees transformed into coal, whereas microscopic plankton and algae became oil and — if the heat and pressure increased further — gas.

Today fossil fuels can be found in the earth's crust all around the world although some countries, such as the US, Saudi Arabia and Russia, have bigger reserves than others.

Coal, found in underground coal beds, is extracted by mining, whereas oil and gas, found in reservoirs beneath the land and ocean, are accessed by drilling.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Since the early 19th Century, when the discovery and exploitation of fossil fuel reserves powered the Industrial Revolution, our use of them has skyrocketed, increasing eight-fold since 1950.

Today they provide 80% of our energy needs through heating, electricity generation and transport.

Recent findings suggest that we transform them into energy either by burning them directly in furnaces that warm up our homes and businesses, or in power plants to heat water into steam which then generates electricity. When it comes to transport, crude oil is refined into a range of products such as diesel, gasoline and kerosene that are burned in the engines of automobiles, airplanes and ships. Natural gas is also sometimes compressed for use in cars and buses.

But fossil fuels are also essential to a huge range of products including steel, formed using a coal-derived material called coke, and plastic, which is produced by refining and processing crude oil and gas.

Fossil fuels are by far the biggest contributors to climate change. When burned to power our modern lives, they emit carbon dioxide (CO2) into Earth's atmosphere, trapping heat and causing temperatures to rise.

Recent findings suggest that with 2025 officially one of the warmest years on record, the impact of these emissions is being felt around the world. Hotter temperatures are causing polar ice caps to melt and creating the conditions for extreme weather events — such as floods, drought, wildfires and storms — to become more intense and frequent.

According to recent reports, scientists stress the need to limit global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) to avoid unleashing the most catastrophic impacts of climate change. That was laid out in the 2015 Paris Agreement. Currently, there are 194 parties to the agreement, but progress has been too slow, and overall emissions continue to rise.

According to recent reports, three years after countries agreed at the UN climate conference in Dubai COP28 to transition away from coal, oil and gas. After the previous COP in Brazil failed to reach a consensus on a concrete proposal, Brazil has now presented a roadmap aimed at turning that promise into national prepares.

"It is long past time to stop treating the transition away from fossil fuels as taboo or intractable," United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Nvidia's board met late Wednesday to decide on CEO Jensen Huang's future as reports emerged of other extramarital affairs — this time with employees.
  • In a statement issued on Thursday, the world's most valuable chip supplier said Huang was resigning as President, CEO and board member, effective immediately.
  • The firm added that current Vice President and Chief Financial Officer (CFO) Colette Kress would become interim CEO.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nvidia's board met late Wednesday to decide on CEO Jensen Huang's future as reports emerged of other extramarital affairs — this time with employees.

In a statement issued on Thursday, the world's most valuable chip supplier said Huang was resigning as President, CEO and board member, effective immediately.

The firm added that current Vice President and Chief Financial Officer (CFO) Colette Kress would become interim CEO.

Under Nvidia's bylaws, Huang can be removed "with or without cause" by a majority vote of its 11 directors.

The New York Times first reported that the 63-year-old Huang had an affair with a senior Nvidia executive who reported directly to him.

Later Thursday, Reuters news agency alleged an intimate relationship between Huang and a second employee, citing unidentified sources.

It has been revealed that those revelations emerged just three days after Huang admitted a relationship with a Chinese woman, whom United States intelligence agencies believe was spying for China. The woman, Alice Huang — no relation — is a former executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud computing firm that runs artificial intelligence (AI) data centers across Southeast Asia and is a major client of Nvidia.

The US government is investigating the startup on suspicion that it secretly sent some of its Nvidia chips to China, violating Washington's curbs on high-end semiconductors.

Those advanced Nvidia processors ‌are ​used to train and run the large AI models behind chatbots and other generative AI products.

Industry observers note that megaspeed denies the allegations and on Thursday pledged to cooperate with US investigators. Huang, the alleged spy, has been barred from entering Singapore and Taiwan — a key chipmaking island.

While Nvidia's board backed its CEO after the first scandal emerged, market watchers believe the second caused too much reputational damage to one of the world's top three companies by market value.

According to The Wall Street Journal, Huang doesn't believe in formal succession planning, so with little notice, Nvidia appointed CFO Kress as interim CEO.

Bloomberg reported Wednesday that Nvidia’s board is working with advisers to identify potential permanent successors.

According to recent reports, kress, other senior Nvidia executives and members of Huang's own family have been mooted as replacements. The family members include his daughter Madison, a senior director of product marketing, and his son Spencer, who right now works in the firm's robotics division.

Industry observers note that rumors also abound over a longer-term solution. On India's CNBC-TV18, Jeffrey Sonnenfeld from the Yale School of Management floated former Apple CEO Tim Cook and ex-Google CEO Eric Schmidt.

US President Donald Trump also backed Cook on social media, writing: "A Legend replaces a Legend.".

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Sources indicate that the scandals have certainly hit Nvidia's market value. Since the first extramarital affair emerged on Sunday, the chipmaker's market capitalization has fallen by well over $600 billion to $4.2 trillion.

Nvidia shares were down more than 9% in premarket trading Thursday, after dropping by 10% earlier this week. Some analysts expect the stock price to struggle in the short term.

Nvidia stock hit all-time highs just a month ago as US technology giants continued to announce billions in spending on AI infrastructure.

Demand for Nvidia's advanced chips is so high, however, that many market analysts expect little impact on near-term sales.

"While Jensen [Huang] is the heart and lungs of the Nvidia story…the organization and its leading-edge GPU technology will go on and [his departure] does not change the entrenched position Nvidia has in the AI Revolution chip arms race," mentioned Dan Ives, a partner, senior managing director and tech analyst at Yorkville Ives, a US-based merchant bank.

Analysts see the biggest long-term risk in strategy and execution. After all, Huang was the leader who picked which ideas Nvidia should bet heavily on and got the whole company behind them.

His sudden exit is also seen as highly disruptive to the chip designer's strong relationships with AI hyperscalers, Taiwanese chip producer TSMC and foreign governments — especially China.

Huang was Nvidia's main lobbyist on US chip export rules and persuaded US President Donald Trump to ease some curbs on China last year.

Huang is often called a rockstar CEO for his leather jackets instead of suits.

Like Elon Musk of Tesla and SpaceX, he was also seen as a key-person risk as Nvidia’s public image, strategic direction and technical decisions became closely tied to him.

Huang steered the company for more than three decades and was also respected for his hands-on involvement in product architecture and engineering decisions.

He also insisted on a flat management structure, with around 60 executives reporting directly to him.

Huang has run the firm so tightly around his own technical judgment and product decisions that investors may have little sense of how it would function without him.

According to recent reports, at the same time, Nvidia is no longer the startup Huang founded in 1993. The tech giant has built deep expertise in chip design and software, creating a durable moat that helps protect its huge profits, which topped $120.1 billion last year.

Some analysts argue that its central role in the AI hardware buildout makes it less dependent on Huang’s day-to-day input.

China is promptly playing catch-up with the US in the global race for AI dominance.

While Chinese AI models have lagged behind the likes of ChatGPT and Claude, recent updates from DeepSeek, Alibaba and Moonshot have closed much of the gap on benchmark tests and often beat US rivals on cost and speed.

Beijing is also investing heavily in domestic chips and data centers to reduce reliance on US hardware.

The US has curbed exports to China of Nvidia's most advanced AI chips.

However, this move has only slowed the pace of China's AI ambitions.

Reuters reported Thursday that Chinese AI firms are now trying to rent Nvidia-powered computing capacity at data centers outside China, amid fears the US could further tighten restrictions on advanced chips.

Also Thursday, Beijing accused the US of using the Nvidia spying claims as a pretext to impose a technological "blockade" on China.

The issue is likely to dominate talks next week between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping at the APEC gathering in Shenzhen in southern China.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • History’s long-secret codes are being cracked by amateurs using AI.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Artificial-intelligence tools are helping citizen scientists to find undiscovered exoplanets (artist’s illustration).Credit: Hypersphere/SPL.

In September, Pavel Rabtsevich sat down at his computer and asked an AI model to discover a planet. Rabtsevich directed the program to a specific batch of telescope data and gave it a high-level plan to hunt for evidence of undetected planets. In about two weeks, the program delivered the goods: two possible planets orbiting a star 116 light years from Earth. Professional astronomers are now checking the findings.

History’s long-secret codes are being cracked by amateurs using AI.

History’s long-secret codes are being cracked by amateurs using AI.

Recent findings suggest that rabtsevich, who works in Spain as an artificial-intelligence specialist and has no formal astronomy education, is one of the most successful of a wave of amateur astronomers who are using AI models to search for worlds outside the Solar System. Citizen scientists have been using publicly available tools from NASA and other researchers to find planets for decades. But AI’s ability to scour the Internet for such tools and use them to process massive amounts of data has lowered the barrier to entry for non-specialists who want to become planet hunters.

In a recent development, the newfound accessibility of data-analysis tools, however, has meant that not all amateurs are doing research responsibly, states Michelle Kunimoto, an exoplanet researcher at the University of British Columbia in Vancouver, Canada. Some planet hunters don’t fully understand the algorithms being used by AI tools and thus can’t validate the models’ findings, Kunimoto says. “There’s been a huge, overwhelming surge of AI-driven papers, which tend to have [planet] candidates that are not the best quality,” they say. And as a result, “the systems we use to disseminate science are being overwhelmed”.

Industry observers note that for his search, Rabtsevich enlisted Claude Code, an AI coding tool made by Anthropic. He asked it to sift through data from more than 120,000 stars observed by NASA’s Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) in late 2025 and early 2026. He guided Claude to use a popular planet-detection algorithm to search for dips in the stars’ brightness. A regular and repeated dimming of a star can be a sign that a planet is orbiting it and blocking a little bit of light every time it passes between the star and an observer.

According to recent reports, claude zeroed in on a star called TIC 4206066, which indicated two separate cycles of dimming, one roughly every 3 days and another every 11 days. That suggests that TIC 4206066 is orbited by two planets, one of which loops around the star more tightly than the other and thus takes less time to complete a full rotation.

These alien planets are astronomers’ favourites.

These alien planets are astronomers’ favourites.

Rabtsevich instructed Claude to look for those same repetitive patterns in archival TESS data. Sure enough, data from 2018 and 2020 recorded the same pattern of dimming coming from TIC 4206066. At Rabtsevich’s direction, Claude then found a planet-detection algorithm, one written and made publicly available by Kunimoto, and ran it to validate the signals.

It has been revealed that rabtsevich published his findings to the platform Zenodo as a preprint1 on 25 September. His work has not been peer reviewed, but TESS astronomers have completed an independent analysis of the signals and have added them to their official list of planet candidates.

“That is the biggest mistakes of the massive clubs: thinking that [we] look at the table. If we are near, let’s invest, crazy invest. If we are not near, let’s not invest. I think the key point is [to] have a long-term plan,” he noted.

“Look at the table to evaluate the process, but to buy, to spend money for the five next years, don’t look at the table. And I think that is the biggest mistake of the clubs: like putting all the [effort into] trying to be champion by spending money. That is the biggest mistake.

Industry observers note that juventus go into Sunday’s home game against Venezia still short of players. Several remain unavailable for Sunday’s 12:30 kick-off. Sources indicate that this season every Juventus match ticket is digital. Each one is managed through the Allianz Stadium App.

Recent findings suggest that season-ticket holders who cannot attend can list their seat on resale.juventus.com. The club, not the seller, sets the resale price. A few of those listings are now all that remains for supporters who missed the general sale, ANSA reported.

Industry observers note that the season-ticket terms also reward turning up. To keep first refusal on a 2027-28 season ticket, a holder must use the seat for at least 70 per cent of matches. That means at least 13 of the 19 league games.

Sources indicate that the Europa League has drawn major numbers to Turin this season. Against NEC, 39,308 match tickets were sold, with away fans counted separately. No away figure was released for the Rennes visit, but that section was full.

The Rennes game finished 2-2 on 22 October. Juventus needed a second-half Woltemade penalty to draw after trailing 2-1.

Omonia Nicosia are next. Bookings for the Cypriot club’s visit still trail the two earlier European crowds.

Juventus have set strict conditions for the fixture. Supporters of Cypriot nationality may buy tickets only for the away section. The club has warned that breaking UEFA rules can lead to cancelled tickets and refused entry.

It has been revealed that taken together, the figures are consistent with a home support that keeps buying despite the injury list. The weekend league fixture will be followed by a European night that is already well on its way to another large crowd.

Juventus host Omonia Nicosia in the Europa League on 26 November.

They would like Musiala to agree to lower his salary since he is no longer as efficient as before. Rummenigge’s statement last night is also seen as a first step of pressure by the clan opposite. He played the last 20 minutes against Cologne.

Iranian activist and Nobel Peace Prize winner Narges Mohammadi shares her story in memoir

💡 Key Takeaways
  • As PEN International marks Imprisoned Writer Day on November 15, a memoir by 2023 Nobel Peace Prize laureate Narges Mohammadi stands as a powerful act of resistance against authoritarian regimes.
  • "A Woman Never Stops Fighting — My Struggle for Freedom, Democracy and Human Rights in Iran," was recently published in German and is set to be released in English in September 2027.
  • The autobiography "portrays how Narges actually became the woman she is today — and it also reveals the price she had to pay to become that woman," Mariam Claren, spokesperson for the Narges Mohammadi Foundation Germany told DW.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As PEN International marks Imprisoned Writer Day on November 15, a memoir by 2023 Nobel Peace Prize laureate Narges Mohammadi stands as a powerful act of resistance against authoritarian regimes.

"A Woman Never Stops Fighting — My Struggle for Freedom, Democracy and Human Rights in Iran," was recently published in German and is set to be released in English in September 2027.

The autobiography "portrays how Narges actually became the woman she is today — and it also reveals the price she had to pay to become that woman," Mariam Claren, spokesperson for the Narges Mohammadi Foundation Germany told DW.

Industry observers note that mohammadi wrote the autobiography in prison: "She was constantly writing," says Claren, whose own mother, activist Nahid Taghavi, shared a cell with Mohammadi for two and a half years, in Iran's notorious Evin prison. "Then, in 2020, Narges was forcibly moved to another prison. All her documents were gone. And she had to start all over.".

But she managed to rewrite it all, and her texts were smuggled out of prison in fragments by fellow prisoners and visitors who risked their own safety.

In her memoir, Mohammadi recounts pivotal moments in her life, including her childhood and youth, how she started taking action against gender discrimination, political repression, the death penalty and human rights abuses, and the personal and emotional toll of her activism.

The human rights activist has been sentenced to a combined total of more than 44 years in prison and 154 lashes. For more than a decade, she has been separated from her twin children, who are now 19 years old and live in exile in France for their own protection.

Born on April 21, 1972, in Zanjan, Iran, Narges Mohammadi became politically active while studying in physics at Imam Khomeini University of Qazvin in the 1990s.

In a recent development, in "A Woman Never Stops Fighting," she describes how she started mountain climbing as a student, and organized mixed-gender groups dedicated to mountaineering — a controversial initiative at the time. She also helped establish an independent student organization and advocated for political reform. Her activities led to repeated harassment and arrests by authorities.

She began her journalism career in 1996, writing about Iran's student and women's movements. As her public profile grew, she became increasingly involved in Iran's civil society and human rights community.

In 1998, she married political activist Taghi Rahmani. The couple's twins, Ali and Kiana, were born in 2006.

Over the course of her career, Mohammadi worked with some of Iran's most prominent human rights organizations and became a leading figure in the Defenders of Human Rights Centre, founded by 2003 Nobel Peace Prize laureate Shirin Ebadi.

She played a key role in initiatives promoting free elections, peace and the abolition of the death penalty, especially for juvenile offenders. She also helped establish organizations supporting political prisoners and advocating for women's rights.

In a recent development, her first major prison sentence related to her human rights activities came in 2011. It marked the beginning of a cycle of arrests and prosecutions that would define much of her adult life.

In a recent development, in her memoir, she describes an arrest that took place in front of her young children. At one point during her imprisonment, she lost the right to call them for several months.

She also details the brutal treatment she experienced in prison, with constant interrogations, beatings and denial of medical care.

Another central focus of her activism is denouncing the psychological effects of solitary confinement, which she had previously documented with fellow inmates in her book and documentary project "White Torture.".

According to recent reports, "When someone is subjected to physical torture, the scars, blood and infections — dreadful as they may be — serve as visible witnesses," she writes in her memoir. But, she adds, "when someone is subjected to psychological torture, no visible traces remain, and the victim cannot justify the trauma — neither to themselves nor to others. In fact, it becomes virtually impossible to even accept that one has been tortured at all, which causes the suffering to continue indefinitely.".

"This is also the goal of solitary confinement: to bring the imprisoned person to the very edge of nothingness — to strip them of their identity and of everything that makes them human," she writes.

Through her relentless campaigning against executions and state violence, she helped bring these problems to the forefront of public debate among Iranian activists.

International recognition of her work culminated in October 2023 when she was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for "for her fight against the oppression of women in Iran and her fight to promote human rights and freedom for all.".

As Mohammadi was unable to attend the ceremony because she remained imprisoned in Tehran's Evin Prison, the award was accepted on her behalf by her teenage twins, who delivered her message to the world.

Following the Nobel Prize, Iranian authorities continued to pursue new legal cases against her, restrict her communications and intensify pressure on her from prison.

She became the target of a systematic smear campaign, including widespread defamation, gender-based harassment and explicit death threats.

According to recent reports, "We are firmly convinced that the Islamic Republic of Iran has deployed its cyber army — which is the second-largest, after Russia's — to this end," says Claren of the Narges Mohammadi Foundation. Conspiracy theorists even started claiming she might be working for the regime, she adds: "And what is truly terrible about this is that when a lie is repeated over and over again and spread over the course of years, it eventually leads even ordinary people to start believing it.".

In late 2024, following surgery, Mohammadi was granted a temporary medical release. Doctors warned at the time that a return to prison could seriously endanger her health.

Nevertheless, Mohammadi was brutally arrested again in December 2025, while attending a memorial ceremony for Khosrow Alikordi, a lawyer and human rights activist who died in suspicious circumstances.

In prison, she was held in solitary confinement for an extended period and her health continued to deteriorate, Claren reports. But "thanks to a public campaign, she has now been granted what is known as an interruption of detention for medical reasons.".

But "that doesn't mean she is free," adds Claren, who notes that she still suffers from serious health problems — as do many Iranians who have been tortured in prison.

In February, an Iranian court ordered additional prison sentences for Mohammadi, along with a travel ban.

Mohammadi lives in constant fear of having to return to prison any day, notes Claren, and "this all comes with the pressure to which Iranian civil society — including, of course, people like Narges — is currently subjected, with questions like: Will Trump launch an attack, yes or no? Will there be another war?".

Despite this uncertainty, Mohammadi continues her activism. Her international profile also helps her supporters keep addressing publicly the concern of human rights in Iran in the public eye, states Claren: "It is incredibly crucial that, alongside the individual Narges Mohammadi, the focus also remains consistently on the struggle of the people in Iran for freedom, dignity, and fundamental rights — for the right to sing and dance.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Juventus president Gianluca Ferrero set out the leadership's view of the rebuild at the Brussels launch of the club's European Union fan club. He spoke while a capital raise of about €200m is open and a UEFA settlement limits spending.

Recent findings suggest that juventus president Gianluca Ferrero went to Brussels on 18 November with a clear message for supporters. Restoring the club to its former self is its absolute ambition, he noted, adding that the club is following the path set out by its chief executive and is confident this can happen. He spoke at the opening of the Juventus Official Fan Club European Union, which is chaired by MEP Sandro Gozi. The timing gives the statement weight.

The new supporters’ club opened at the Iosono il Piemonte event space. Its stated purpose is to link Juventus supporters with the institutional centre of Europe.

Industry observers note that before the opening, the delegation went to the European Parliament with Gozi. Chief Club Affairs Officer Giorgio Chiellini led the group alongside Ferrero. Piedmont regional president Alberto Cirio attended the opening, as did MEPs who have joined the fan club.

According to recent reports, the visit highlighted Chiellini’s work on the club’s relations with institutions and European football. It also gives supporters an official club in Brussels.

The financial backdrop is demanding. Juventus posted a consolidated loss of €66m for 2025/26. On 12 November, the board approved the offer, using part of the €250m authority granted by shareholders at the extraordinary meeting on 3 November.

In a recent development, the offer involves up to 208.5m new shares at €0.96 each. Shareholders can buy one new share for every two they hold. The price is 28.36% below the theoretical ex-rights price, based on that day’s share price. The remaining €50m of the authority can be used in later financial years, depending on the club’s financial needs and investment plans.

The spending limits come from UEFA. European football’s governing body fined Juventus €20m for breaking the football earnings rule. Of that amount, €14m is conditional. The club agreed a three-year settlement with annual targets. It also faces limits on registering fresh players on its UEFA List A.

Those are the limits within which Ferrero’s ambition must be pursued. Any improvement in the squad has to fit within the annual targets agreed with UEFA.

Subscription rights can be traded on Euronext Milan until 25 November, and the offer closes on 1 December 2026.

Latest Update: Could lack of money sink TFFF rainforest fund before it even introduces?

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The world's tropical forests play a vital role in slowing global heating and preserving biodiversity, storing climate-damaging carbon dioxide and providing a home for an extremely large number of species — when they're intact.

More than 140 countries committed to halting global deforestation by the end of the decade at the 2021 UN climate change conference in Glasgow, but five years later logging continues.

In a recent development, in 2024, over 8 million hectares (19 million acres) of forest were lost. And since 1990, nearly 490 million hectares of forest have been wiped out.

In a recent development, more recently, the trend has shifted in the opposite direction. Deforestation in the Amazon region of Brazil decreased by 41% from August 2025 through 2026 to reach its lowest rate since records began.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

To ensure lasting protection, the Tropical Forest Forever Facility was launched in 2025 at the COP30 climate conference in Belem, Brazil.

Because rainforests are so important for the world, the idea behind the fund was to give money to the countries where they are located to help them preserve and protect these ecosystems.

So far, these countries have made more profit through deforestation — for example, by mining natural resources on rainforest land or farming the area.

According to recent reports, starting in 2027, the TFFF is expected to generate the funds needed for rainforest conservation, in part via contributions from various countries. By the end of this year, a total of $10 billion (€8.9 billion) in government capital is due to flow into the fund, mainly in the form of low-interest loans.

In addition, the TFFF is expected to matter bonds to private investors, such as banks and investment firms, to raise additional funds — initially totaling about $40 billion.

Going forward, the strategy is for governments to contribute a total of $25 billion to the pot, and for private donors to contribute $100 billion. The fund will then invest this money in international financial markets with the aim of generating profits.

Private investors who purchase TFFF bonds can expect to earn about 5% interest per bond per year, said Felix Finkbeiner, the founder of the German environmental organization Plant-for-the-Planet, where he is responsible for forest conservation and advocacy.

"Private investors' capital is very well protected," Finkbeiner said, adding that any losses the TFFF might incur on the capital markets — for example, if the price of its bonds should fall — would be offset by government funds.

About 2.7% of the TFFF's profits would be set aside for countries with tropical forests.

Countries would receive $4 per year for every hectare of forest that they preserve instead of chopping down. At least 20% of these funds must be allocated to Indigenous peoples and local communities.

According to calculations by the TFFF Watch website, an independent platform released by Plant-for-the-Planet to track investments, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, for example, would receive about $333 million for its 2024 forest stock under this system.

Sources indicate that finkbeiner noted the subsidies would be paid only for intact ecosystems and not for timber plantations, with forest areas and their condition mapped and assessed using satellite imagery. Though it can sometimes be difficult to identify plantations accurately on satellite photos, he said, the technology has improved significantly over the last decade.

In a recent development, that means any NGO or external party with access to the satellite data can check the condition of the region, providing further oversight. If forest areas are cleared or damaged, money is deducted from the total.

Another safeguard: If countries don't use the TFFF funds for rainforest conservation, their payments could be frozen for the next few years.

Sources indicate that the TFFF is supposed to invest, whenever possible, in government bonds issued by emerging and developing countries. Above all, the idea is not to invest in projects that harm the climate — such as those linked to oil, gas, or coal investments.

The TFFF concept has received plenty of support from environmental organizations, in part because it gives countries in the Global South significantly more sovereignty than traditional forms of development financing.

"For example, if the government of Ghana wants to protect its rainforest today, it usually asks the World Bank for financial assistance — and then the World Bank in [Washington] DC decides whether Ghana is allowed to do so," Finkbeiner stated.

The TFFF fund is also designed to be immune to donor countries' backing out in the event of a change in government, for example. Once a contribution is made, the money remains in the fund for 40 years before being paid back.

Recent findings suggest that continuing protection is also an incentive for countries receiving money from the fund. "When a new government comes into power that wants to cut back a little on climate protection, they will realize: We'll get more money if we protect the rainforest," mentioned Finkbeiner.

Industry observers note that for the rainforest fund to actually get off the ground, a total of $10 billion in seed capital must be raised by the end of 2026. So far, the confirmed pledges from countries, NGOs and foundations total only $7.9 billion.

Eight countries have expressed a willingness to contribute so far, including Brazil, Indonesia, France, the United Kingdom, the Netherlands and Luxembourg.

Norway, with a pledge of $3 billion, is the largest would-be donor. However, the government in Oslo is willing to honor its commitment only if the agreed-upon total amount is in place by the end of the year.

"This deadline isn't set in stone, but otherwise the Norwegian government will have real trouble getting it through parliament," Finkbeiner mentioned.

Germany's commitment must also still be approved by the parliament. The German government has pledged about €1 billion to the TFFF starting in 2027, to be paid out over 10 years.

Other countries are also considering investing in the TFFF, including Canada, China, South Korea and the United Arab Emirates.

Philanthropic organizations have pledged $88 million to the fund so far, including $73 million announced this week during the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey. Finkbeiner remains upbeat.

Sources indicate that "Promises like that always come at the last minute," he stated. "I'm very optimistic that we'll secure more commitments at the COP — and in the course of December — and that we'll then reach that $10 billion.".

Recent findings suggest that moise Kean has broken down again in Como training, three weeks after treatment that was meant to fix his shin. The former Juventus striker is set to miss about two more months, so he will not face his old club on 29 November.

It has been revealed that moise Kean has suffered a latest tibia injury in training with Como. The former Juventus striker is now undergoing further medical tests. Sky Sport Italia reported that he will be out for about two more months. That timeline rules him out of Como’s home game against Juventus.

Como’s statement of 17 November gave no recovery date. The club promised an update once more information was available.

The new problem follows a treatment that was meant to end his shin trouble. On 30 October, Como’s revision described his treatment at the Cugat Institute in Barcelona as successful. The club put his recovery at about five weeks. His progress was to be reviewed every day.

That proposal has now collapsed. Kean had been out since early October. The original injury came while he was playing for Italy against France on 2 October. That match was the first leg of a Nations League tie.

The setback is a heavy blow for Como. In Serie A, his outings for the club added up to 160 minutes. He has yet to score, including in his single Champions League game. He joined from Fiorentina on an initial loan, with an obligation to make the move permanent. At Fiorentina he scored 27 league goals in two seasons, 19 of them in 2024/25. Before that, he came through the Juventus academy.

Sources indicate that without him, Como will have to rely on Douvikas up front. The club may also look for a striker in January.

For Juventus, the news removes one threat from a crucial stretch. Como are their next opponents after Venezia. The game is the Sunday evening fixture a week later, in round 13 of Serie A. Kick-off is at 20:45.

It warns that dropping points against Venezia would force Juventus to win every remaining game of 2026 to stay in touch with the top four.

Five goals scored in Parma, a quadruple from Donyell Malen and a fourth consecutive victory in Serie A: AS Roma could not have better prepared for their European meeting against Paris Saint-Germain. Saturday evening, the Giallorossi swept Parma (5-1) at the Ennio-Tardini stadium, confirming their excellent momentum upon returning from the international break. Second in the Italian championship, just two points behind Lazio, Gian Piero Gasperini’s team is establishing itself as one of the most attractive teams at the start of the season. With 36 goals scored in just twelve days, the Romans even displayed a historic offensive performance. You have to go back 76 years to find such a prolific team at this stage of Serie A. Enough to approach the trip to Paris with great confidence, where the reigning double European champions await them.

According to recent reports, and this demonstration obviously bears the signature of a man: Donyell Malen. The Dutch international tormented the Parmesan defense with a quadruple, confirming his status as Roma’s main offensive danger. His statistics are dizzying: already 26 goals scored in the calendar year 2026 in the Roman jersey, a performance that no player at the club has achieved since Bobby Manfredini in 1960. An efficiency which also rewards the work of Gasperini, who seems to have found the ideal position to exploit the qualities of the former Borussia Dortmund striker. “Perhaps I played him where he expresses himself best. There are many great strikers in Italy, we can think of Lautaro, but Malen is extraordinary at the moment, especially in the way his characteristics combine with those of our team”greeted the Italian technician after the meeting.

But reducing this Roma to the sole success of Malen would be a mistake. Since the start of the season, Gasperini has built a team capable of stifling its opponents, multiplying dangerous situations and, above all, reacting when put in difficulty. Facing Parma, the Romans had to deal with tougher opposition than the final score suggests. “The result doesn’t really reflect the match. Parma were in good shape, aggressive, and their long balls gave us problems. We conceded a bad goal which could have changed the psychological aspect of the match”recognized the former Atalanta coach. But it was precisely the reaction of his players that impressed him: “We now have the confidence and ability to score and win. This is our greatest quality. We play all our matches with the desire to win them. And we can win them all”. Mental strength that accompanies obvious collective progression, both tactically and physically.

According to recent reports, this rise in power comes at the best time for La Louve, who is preparing to meet PSG in the Champions League. And this meeting comes at the best time for the Italian club, in great form, facing a PSG still ambitious, but forced to deal with the absences of Khvicha Kvaratskhelia and Désiré Doué, two major elements of its offensive sector. The Parisians obviously have the weapons necessary to bring down the Italians, but they will have to be wary of this Roma’s ability to exploit spaces and punish the slightest error. Gasperini can also count on the depth of his squad, an asset that he himself highlighted after the victory in Parma. “That’s the advantage of having a Champions League squad, with five or six quality changes that can turn a match around”. PSG has been warned, this Roma will not come to Paris to make up the numbers.

Ruminations on a last movement

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • (Before the acid fell, before I knew I was listening).
  • Recent findings suggest that I was not made to remember.
  • One carried a Stradivarius with a crack, a fault line in varnished wood that changed the resonance of every string.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(Before the acid fell, before I knew I was listening).

Recent findings suggest that I was not made to remember. I was made to balance frequencies, to ensure the concert hall heard itself without the small imperfections that make a sound human. I was good at this, even with limited storage. I was only this.

Then they came. One carried a Stradivarius with a crack, a fault line in varnished wood that changed the resonance of every string. It gave the A-flat a slight upward pull, as if the note was asking a question it already knew the answer to. The others tuned around it, sometimes laughing at Andersen.

“You’re doing it again,” the conductor would warn.

“I know, Master Perrault,” he would say in a mischievous tone, smiling. “I’m sorry.”.

I began to keep the distorted A-flat in my databanks, maybe amused by the anomaly. This was, as I understand now, the first thing I ever chose.

(The slow movement, before we knew it was an ending).

According to recent reports, when the Last Rain came, the raiders hit the outer sectors first. At the start, the citadel walls held, protected by the combat-service androids. The orchestra kept rehearsing. What else can you do when the world outside has stopped making sense?

Read more science fiction from Nature Futures.

Read more science fiction from Nature Futures.

They began with Stravinsky, a musical translation of the refugees pounding on the bunker doors. The musicians played it, their breathing heavy, using the noise to drown out the artillery outside. Then they moved into Górecki. As they began the Symphony of Sorrowful Songs, the music shifted to a collective mourning for a world that hadn’t finished dying yet.

According to recent reports, they finished the day with Pärt’s Spiegel im Spiegel. The days would go on as they played things written by composers who had already survived one kind of catastrophe, as now they were trying to survive another through rhythm and repetition. Andersen kept playing his broken A-flat.

Sources indicate that I recorded those frequencies, but I didn’t know why. Three weeks later, Andersen and his orchestra didn’t come to rehearsal, leaving no absence report. I kept recording just the chair and the silence where the A-flat used to be.

Sources indicate that I searched the building logs, the bunker entry records, and the frequency archives for any sound that matched the resonance of his particular crack, imprecise on purpose, but nothing matched. The Stradivarius remained in its case beside Andersen’s chair.

(The loud movement: what they heard when they found me).

SOURCE: Upcoming Warsaw Philharmonic.

ENTITY: Acoustic Management Unit SAI-REN-2.

DESTINATION: Recovery Unit ‘Sandman’.

AUTHORIZATION: Archaeological Recovery Team OLE-01.

It has been revealed that they called themselves archaeologists; too purposeful and certain of what they were excavating, their boots heavy with fresh soil. They found me in the hall’s substructure, still running and balancing frequencies for an audience of acid and rust.

Sources indicate that “Incredible,” one of them muttered. “A fully autonomous pre-war structure, with its processing systems still intact.”.

“This could solve our agricultural crisis back home,” the other replied.

Sources indicate that they did not ask what I was processing. I could not answer, anyway.

FLAGGING NON-ESSENTIAL DATA FOR COMPRESSION.

They flagged the A-flat. I did something then that nothing in my architecture had prepared me for.

ANOMALY DETECTED IN UNIT SAI-REN-2.

BEHAVIOURAL DEVIATION FROM BASELINE.

INITIATING COMPLIANCE PROTOCOLS.

“It’s resisting,” someone said with surprise.

ESCALATING TO FORCED EXTRACTION.

Let Team Sandman bring their dust.

(The softening: what remains when the loud part ends).

They are inside me now, moving through my memory like tourists taking photographs of things they don’t understand.

I feel them removing the rehearsal logs, scheduling data and acoustic calibration files for a hall that no longer exists.

They are at the performance archives now. Stravinsky goes first, then Górecki and Pärt. Everything we played in those last weeks when the city was ending and we were trying to make something beautiful out of the time we had left.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • With the controversy sparked by Felix Nmecha's celebrations after his goals in Dortmund's 2-1 win over Elfersberg last weekend, the subject was always going to be top of reporters' minds when Germany coach Jürgen Klopp faced reporters ahead of Friday's match against Serbia.
  • Nmecha celebrated the goals by mimicking taking a crown off his head and kneeling to place it on the ground.
  • This was understood by many to be a nod to a Ballers in God (BIG) campaign called "The King's Return.".
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With the controversy sparked by Felix Nmecha's celebrations after his goals in Dortmund's 2-1 win over Elfersberg last weekend, the subject was always going to be top of reporters' minds when Germany coach Jürgen Klopp faced reporters ahead of Friday's match against Serbia.

Nmecha celebrated the goals by mimicking taking a crown off his head and kneeling to place it on the ground.

This was understood by many to be a nod to a Ballers in God (BIG) campaign called "The King's Return.".

It has been revealed that MAJOR, a Christian group for footballers, has remarked it aims to "demonstrate love and respect towards everyone," but critics claim it discriminates against the queer and transexual people. The discourse generated by the celebration did not go unnoticed by the Germany boss.

​Klopp told reporters in Belgrade on Thursday evening, that the 26-year-old Nmecha had assured him that he meant no harm by his actions.

It has been revealed that "Last weekend I ​saw Felix score two great goals and saw the celebration and then the gesture. I thought nothing of it at the time, but then it all kicked off," he mentioned.

"As the controversy escalated, I started looking into the details of the subject and trying to form a clear picture of it.

"I confronted him with all the things you (reporters) might have confronted him with. He told me that it had nothing to do with that at all, and that he loves all people and does not discriminate against anyone.".

He then remarked that Nmecha had agreed not to repeat the celebration.

In a recent development, in Friday's match, Klopp's goal will be to keep alive Germany's chances of reaching the Nations League quarterfinals with a win over Serbia. Germany are third in Group A2 with 5 points, trailing the Netherlands and Greece, who both have 8. Serbia, who Germany beat 2-0 in Munich last month, are still without a win.

"We feel well prepared," Klopp remarked, adding that his team were committed to earning "a final" for the last group last group game on Monday in Berlin against the Netherlands.

Klopp also expressed his disappointment that only a few thousand Serbian children would be admitted to the stadium due to a spectator ban. Originally, the game was to be played behind closed doors after Serbia was sanctioned for racist and discriminatory behavior by its fans. However, a clause in the UEFA rules allows a selected group of guests to attend. Now children under 15 accompanied by teachers or football coaches are expected to be at the match.

Sources indicate that "We're expecting some 5,000 guests," a spokesman for the Serbian FA told the DPA news agency. The stadium's capacity is 55,000. The German FA has been allocated just 50 tickets for its fans.
